background.definition: Blastomycosis, also known as Gilchrist disease, is an uncommon, chronic, granulomatous fungal disease caused by the dimorphic fungus Blastomyces dermatitidis.

list.listitem: In endemic regions (Mississippi and Ohio River valleys, Great Lakes and St. Lawrence River regions), the annual incidence is 1.3 to 1.4 per 100,000 persons.
Incidence may approach 75 per 100,000 persons in hyperendemic regions.
Most patients are 30 to 69 years of age. Perhaps because of occupational and recreational exposure, men are affected 15 times more often than women.
Blastomycosis is caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis, a dimorphic fungus.
The fungus affects both immunocompetent and immunocompromised individuals.
When soil containing the organism fungal content is disturbed, spores are aerosolized.
A granulomatous reaction may destroy inhaled spores and prevent disease. Although a humoral response develops, cellular immunity is the major factor in determining whether disease develops.
Spores not killed by the alveolar macrophages transform into yeast cells. The yeast form may spread via the blood and lymphatics to other organs.
A pyogranulomatous response, distinctive of blastomycosis, consisting of macrophages and polymorphonuclear cells may develop. Local necrosis and fibrosis may also occur.
Blastomyces may also spread hematogenously to extra-thoracic sites, infecting skin (20%-40%), bone (up to 25%), and the CNS (5%-10%).

list.listitem: Blastomycosis is endemic in the Mississippi and Ohio River Valleys, the Great Lakes region, and areas bordering the St. Lawrence River.
Fewer than half of the individuals infected by blastomyces develop clinical disease. When blastomycosis becomes symptomatic, it may take on an acute or chronic clinical course.
The acute form may present with signs and symptoms similar to those of bacterial pneumonia: cough, fever, and chills.

The chronic form is more common, as patients present with persistent productive cough, intermittent low-grade fevers, chest pain, and hemoptysis. Fatigue, malaise, and weight loss also accompany the chronic form, mimicking tuberculosis or malignancy.
Of patients developing clinical symptoms, 70% to 90% have pulmonary manifestations. Of those infected, 25% to 40% go on to develop extrapulmonary manifestations, primarily cutaneous blastomycosis.

In 2 small case series (61 and 36 patients), patients with blastomycosis reported the following symptoms: productive cough with or without hemoptysis (80%), fatigue (82%), dyspnea (48%), fever (73%), weight loss (68%), night sweats (68%), and chest pain (43%). About a quarter had skin manifestations.
When blastomycosis is suspected, order sputum stain and urine antigen testing.

Direct visualization of the yeast form in tissues or sputum is sufficient for rapid diagnosis; culture is used to confirm the diagnosis but can take several weeks. The sensitivity of direct visualization of the yeast form is 50% to 90% (the specificity is unreported).

Urinary antigen aids in rapid detection of infection and in monitoring response to therapy. It is 92% sensitive and over 98% specific in patients without fungal infection, but it exhibits a high cross-reactivity in those with histoplasmosis and paracoccidioidomycosis.
Serological testing is insensitive (16%-40%) and lacks specificity.

Imaging results are nonspecific for blastomycosis. The most common radiographic finding in blastomycosis is airspace consolidation (25%-75%); other findings include masses (up to 31%), miliary pattern (11%-28%), and nodules with diffuse reticulonodular pattern (6%-9%). A fibrotic interstitial structure, and rarely cavitary lesions, may be seen. Multiple findings are seen in up to 65% of cases.
CT or MRI may detect skeletal involvement in patients with extrapulmonary blastomycosis.
Extensive investigation for an underlying immunodeficiency is not indicated for blastomycosis.
Suspect blastomycosis in patients living in an endemic region presenting with chronic cough or symptoms of pneumonia.
Initial diagnostic testing should consist of sputum stain and urine antigen testing.
Empiric treatment with antifungal therapy in cases of antibiotic-resistant pneumonia is reasonable for those in endemic or epidemic situations.

The CDC provides an algorithm that recommends considering blastomycosis in persons with CAP of unknown etiology not responding to antibiotics, or is linked to a known blastomycosis outbreak, or has typical skin lesions. Enzyme immunoassay testing or urine is the initial step. If positive, diagnose pulmonary blastomycosis. If negative but high degree of suspicion order additional tests (sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage culture and microscopy; skin biopsy if lesion exists for histopathology; or serologic antibody tests).
The drug of choice is amphotericin B and/or an azole, depending on the severity of disease, type of infection, and immune status of the patient. summarizes the treatment recommendations. B

Treatment for blastomycosis varies with severity and dissemination of the infection, immune status, and pregnancy state. Extrapulmonary disease is treated the same as pulmonary, with the exception of osteoarticular or CNS infections.
No guidelines exist to assess severity of illness.
Due to relapses, all patients with blastomycosis should have close follow-up for 6 months to confirm disease resolution. See for specific treatment regimens.

There are only two randomized trials of blastomycosis treatment, each evaluating different azoles and with a total of 120 patients. Amphotericin B is considered the mainstay of therapy, giving cure without relapse in 75% to 90% of patients receiving cumulative doses above 1 g. Ketoconazole has a cure rate of 70% to 85%, and itraconazole has a 95% cure rate.
Amphotericin B is used in patients who have severe blastomycosis and in patients with CNS involvement.
Patients with osteoarticular disease should be treated for a minimum of 12 months.
Patients with relapse should receive life-long daily itraconazole.
Immunodeficient patients should also receive life-long daily itraconazole suppressive therapy.
Intervention may require oxygen, bronchoscopy, or ventilatory support similar to that required in severe pneumonia of other etiologies.
Many infections are asymptomatic; most patients who present have pneumonia, which may progress to ARDS. C
As many as 30% of patients develop disseminated disease involving multiple organs. B
Relapse may occur, even in the immunocompetent patient, months after appropriate treatment, so patients need follow-up for at least 6 months. C
Monitor serum itraconazole level 2 weeks into treatment. C
The lipid formulation of amphotericin B (3-5 mg/kg per day up to 1.5-2.5 g total dose) is the drug of choice in pregnant women.
Azoles should be avoided in pregnancy due to possible teratogenicity.
Children are rarely diagnosed, except during outbreaks, when all ages and sexes are equally likely to be infected. Clinical spectrum of disease is similar to that in adults.

Life-threatening or CNS disease should be treated with amphotericin B. Dosing options are: deoxycholate amphotericin B 0.7 to 1 mg/kg per day, or lipid formulation of amphotericin B 3 to 5 mg/kg per day for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by itraconazole 10 mg/kg per day for 12 months.
Non-life-threatening or non-CNS disease should be treated with itraconazole at 5 to 7 mg/kg day, and 10 mg/kg per day for 6 to 12 months.
The azole dose in children should not exceed 400 mg/day.

feature.caption: Treatment of Blastomycosis.
feature.feature_body:
Condition Antifungal Therapy Comment
Pulmonary or disseminated extrapulmonary disease Mild to moderate disease: itraconazole 200 mg PO TID for 3 days, then 200 mg PO BID for 6-12 months Patients with osteoarticular blastomycosis should be treated for a minimum of 12 months. Monitor serum itraconazole level 2 weeks into treatment
Moderate to severe disease: amphotericin B (lipid 3-5 mg/kg/day, or deoxycholate 0.7-1 mg/kg/day for 1-2 weeks or until clinical improvement noted), then itraconazole 200 mg PO TID for 3 days, then 200 mg PO BID for 6-12 months
CNS disease Amphotericin B (lipid 5 mg/kg/day) for 4-6 weeks, then an oral azole (fluconazole 800 mg QD, itraconazole 200 mg BID/TID, or voriconazole 200-400 mg BID) for at least 12 months or until resolution of CNS abnormalities
Disease relapse Itraconazole 200 mg/PO daily life-long suppressive therapy Monitor serum itraconazole level 2 weeks into treatment
Disease in patients with irreversible immunosupression Itraconazole 200 mg/PO daily life-long suppressive therapy Monitor serum itraconazole level 2 weeks into treatment
